Roman Hindi has no standard spelling: Google's Dakshina dataset averages 1.8 attested Roman spellings per Hindi word, so pick one form, such as shubhkamnayein, and keep it.
In our sample lines, English runs from 12% of the words for parents to 40% for a partner.

faqs.question: How do you spell Diwali ki shubhkamnayein in English letters?
faqs.answer: There is no official spelling, so pick one and keep it: shubhkamnayein is the fullest and reads most careful to elders, while shubhkamnaye is common in casual chats. Google Research's Dakshina dataset records an average of 1.8 attested Roman spellings per Hindi word, so variation is normal, not a mistake.

faqs.question: Should I write Deepawali or Deepavali in a Hinglish message?
faqs.answer: Either is understood; Deepawali follows the common Hindi pronunciation and Deepavali follows the Sanskrit form. The only rule that matters is using one spelling throughout a single message.

faqs.question: Is it okay to send my parents a Hinglish Diwali wish instead of pure Hindi?
faqs.answer: Yes, if they text you in Roman Hindi already. Keep aap, keep the Hindi verb endings and limit English to everyday nouns like photo or recipe; our parents' sample line uses English for only 2 of 17 words.

faqs.question: Can I type h instead of hai in a Diwali wish?
faqs.answer: In a friends' group chat, yes. To a parent, a boss or a relative, type hai in full, because the one-letter form reads as hurried in a message meant to show care.

faqs.question: Is Diwali mubarak a correct greeting?
faqs.answer: Yes. Mubarak is a Persian borrowing that Hindi dictionaries record as meaning blessed or happy in greetings, and many Urdu-leaning and North Indian households use Diwali mubarak naturally. Use it if the person you are wishing uses it too.

faqs.question: When should I send Hinglish Diwali wishes in 2027?
faqs.answer: Diwali (Lakshmi Puja) falls on Friday 29 October 2027, with Dhanteras on 27 October and Bhai Dooj on 31 October. Send family wishes that morning, friends' group wishes after the evening puja, and office wishes on Thursday 28 October during working hours.

faqs.question: Why do Indians mix Hindi and English when they text?
faqs.answer: Bilingual speakers switch languages within a sentence as a normal part of speech, and they type it the way they say it. A 2014 Microsoft Research India study of Facebook comments found 23.7% of Hindi-frame sentences carried at least one English word, and Roman script far outnumbered Devanagari on the pages it sampled.

faqs.question: How do I wish my boss Happy Diwali in Hinglish without sounding too casual?
faqs.answer: Use aap, open with Sir or Ma'am, and keep the Hindi for the polite parts: a line like 'aapko aur ghar mein sabko Shubh Deepawali' works. Leave out yaar, bro and any joke about bonuses.

faqs.question: Should I use tu, tum or aap in a Diwali wish?
faqs.answer: Use aap for parents, elders, relatives and your manager; tum for a partner or a sibling you already address that way; tu only where it is already mutual, such as a best friend. Switching to tu just for the festival reads as a slight, not as warmth.

faqs.question: Can I put a Hinglish wish inside a Diwali card instead of a text?
faqs.answer: Yes. SubhSandesh's Diwali card lets you write a wish for each diya, a tag on the diya at their door and a letter in a shagun liffafa, in any mix of Hindi and English. It opens from a private link in any phone browser with no app.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Hinglish Diwali Wishes, Typed the Way People Actually Text

Hinglish Diwali wishes work when the Hindi grammar of the sentence (the verb, the *ke liye*, the *hai*) stays put and English words drop into it, typed in Roman letters on a phone keyboard. Below are 24 original lines sorted by recipient, plus the spelling and register rules that decide whether a line reads as warm or as a forward.

Two SubhSandesh numbers explain why typing matters: 48.3% of shared pages are opened on a phone (measured 24 September 2026), and in Raksha Bandhan 2026, our nearest festival analogue (n = 89 pages), 49.4% of greeting pages were built on the day itself. Expect these wishes to be thumb-typed on 29 October 2027.

## What counts as a Hinglish Diwali wish, according to the 2025 Bhasha study?

A Hinglish wish is a Hindi sentence frame carrying English words, not English with one Hindi word sprinkled on top. Anmol Sahni's [2025 peer-reviewed Hinglish analysis in *Bhasha*](https://edizionicafoscari.it/it/edizioni/riviste/bhasha/2025/1/code-switching-in-south-asia-comparing-the-equival/) finds that in a sentence like "Ram highly qualified hai", Hindi supplies the grammatical scaffolding (the verb *hai*, the postposition *mai*) while English supplies lexical pieces such as adjectives.

That is the practical test for a Diwali line. "Is baar ki Diwali full grand hogi" is Hinglish; "Wishing you a grand Diwali, ji" is English with a Hindi garnish.

## How do people actually type Roman Hindi? 1.8 spellings per word

There is no fixed spelling. Google Research's [Dakshina dataset paper (LREC 2020)](https://aclanthology.org/2020.lrec-1.294/) states that Brahmic-script languages have no standard romanisation in common use, and its Hindi lexicon averages 1.8 attested romanisations per native word. The paper's own example: one Hindi word for corruption was typed at least four different ways in a single blog comment thread.

Roman script is also the default. In the [2014 Microsoft Research India study of Hindi-English mixing on Facebook](https://aclanthology.org/W14-3914/), comments on Narendra Modi's page contained 43,804 Roman-script words against 9,509 in Devanagari, and on Amitabh Bachchan's page 38,144 against 2,661. Spelling choices that keep a Diwali line readable:

- Pick one spelling of the greeting per message: *Deepawali* or *Deepavali*, never both.
- Write *shubhkamnayein* in full for elders; *shubhkamnaye* is common but reads hurried.
- Type *hai*, not *h*, to anyone older than you. *Aap*, not *ap*, to a parent.
- Capitalise names and relation words (Mummy, Bhai, Nani) and nothing else.

## 24 Hinglish Diwali wishes by recipient

All 24 lines are original. Each group gives the pronoun, the English share and the send day in Diwali week 2027 (27 to 31 October).

### 1. For Mummy and Papa

**Pronoun:** *aap*. **English:** everyday words only (photo, recipe, list). **Send:** Lakshmi Puja morning, Friday 29 October 2027.

- Mummy Papa, aapke haath ke besan ladoo ki recipe ab bhi mere phone ke notes mein save hai. Is saal main try karungi, Happy Diwali.
- Papa, Lakshmi puja ki thali ki photo zaroor bhejna, office se live dekhni hai mujhe. Aap dono ko Shubh Deepawali.
- Mummy, safai ka poora load akele mat uthana. List mere saath share karo, aadha kaam mera.
- Aap dono ka ashirwad hi mera asli annual bonus hai. Diwali ki dher saari shubhkamnayein, Mummy Papa.

### 2. For a brother or sister

**Pronoun:** *tu* if you already use it, else *tum*. **English:** freely. **Send:** Choti Diwali, Thursday 28 October 2027.

- Oye bhai, is baar rangoli ka design main choose karungi, tu sirf colour bharega. Deal? Happy Diwali.
- Didi, tere bina ghar ki string lights koi seedhi nahi lagata. Jaldi aa ja, Happy Diwali.
- Chhote, ek din phone side mein rakh aur mithai ka dabba mere liye bhi bachana. Shubh Deepawali.
- Bhai, Dhanteras pe jo bhi naya aaye, usme mera hissa pakka. Happy Diwali, sabse annoying sibling.

### 3. For a best friend or the group chat

**Pronoun:** *tu* or *yaar*. **English:** up to half the line. **Send:** Friday 29 October 2027, after the puja.

- Bro, Diwali party ka plan aaj final kar, warna har saal ki tarah raat 11 baje "kahan ho" wale messages chalenge.
- Group ke saare pagal logon ko Happy Diwali. Is saal kaju katli ke last piece pe fight nahi, toss hoga.
- Yaar, [your shared memory] wali Diwali yaad hai? Wahi energy, same team, Happy Diwali.
- Diwali pe ghar aa ja, mummy ne already tere liye extra chakli bana di hai. No excuses.

### 4. For a partner, near or far

**Pronoun:** *tum*. **English:** up to half, endearments included. **Send:** 29 October 2027, after the diyas are lit.

- Tumhare saath pehli Diwali hai, toh diye bhi do jalenge, ek tumhare naam ka. Happy Diwali, jaan.
- Iss baar Diwali pe meri ek hi wish hai: next year same balcony, same lights, aur tum mere side mein.
- Tum Bengaluru mein, main Lucknow mein, par 7 baje video call pe diya saath jalana hai. Okay? Happy Diwali, love.
- Tumhari wajah se mera poora saal thoda zyada roshan raha. Shubh Deepawali, meri favourite insaan.

### 5. For the office group or a manager

**Pronoun:** *aap*. **English:** about a third, Hindi for the politeness. **Send:** Thursday 28 October 2027, office hours.

- Team, is saal ki saari late-night deadlines ke liye thank you. Aap sabko aur ghar walon ko Happy Diwali.
- Sir, aapko aur ghar mein sabko Shubh Deepawali. Is hafte laptop band rakhiyega, aapne yeh break kamaya hai.
- Happy Diwali everyone! Mithai ka dabba pantry mein rakh diya hai, pehle aao pehle pao.
- Ma'am, poore saal ki guidance ke liye shukriya. Aapki Diwali shaant aur roshan ho.

### 6. For the relatives' family group

**Pronoun:** *aap*, plural. **English:** almost none. **Send:** Govardhan Puja, Saturday 30 October 2027.

- Saare chacha-chachi aur mausa-mausi ko pranam aur Happy Diwali. Is baar ek din ke liye sab milte hain na?
- Nani, aapki diye wali kahani ab main bachchon ko sunati hoon. Diwali mubarak, aapka ashirwad chahiye.
- Family group ke sabhi logon ko Shubh Deepawali. Forward wala video mat bhejna, apni ek photo bhejna.
- Bua ji, aapke ghar ki Govardhan puja ki bahut yaad aa rahi hai. Is baar video call pe dikhana.

## Where should the English go in a Hinglish wish? The 23.7% pattern

Put English inside a Hindi sentence, not the reverse. In the Facebook study, 23.7% of Hindi-frame sentences carried at least one English word, against only 7.2% of English-frame sentences carrying Hindi, and 17.2% of all posts showed some mixing.

The same study notes that many Hindi nouns embedded in English are kinship terms, greetings and address forms. That is why "Happy Diwali, Nani" feels natural and "may your ghar be roshan" does not. To write your own:

- Start with a Hindi frame ending in *hai* or *ho*.
- Swap in at most two English nouns or adjectives (photo, plan, lights).
- Close with one greeting: *Happy Diwali* is casual, *Shubh Deepawali* warmer and more formal.
- Use *mubarak* only if the person uses it. [Wiktionary's Hindi entry for मुबारक](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AE%E0%A5%81%E0%A4%AC%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%B0%E0%A4%95) records it as a Persian borrowing meaning "blessed, happy (used in greetings)".

The plural *shubhkamnayein* comes from शुभकामना, which [Wiktionary glosses as "best wishes, congratulations"](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E0%A4%B6%E0%A5%81%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%A8%E0%A4%BE), a feminine noun. That is why it takes *ki* (*Diwali ki shubhkamnayein*), never *ka*.

## Which Hinglish register fits whom, compared

Each row takes one sample line from this page and counts its English words. "Diwali" counts as neither language.

| Recipient | Pronoun | English words in our sample line | Greeting spelling | Send on (2027) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Parents | aap | 2 of 17 words, 12% ("annual bonus" line) | Shubhkamnayein, *hai* in full | Fri 29 Oct, morning |
| Sibling | tu / tum | 5 of 17 words, 29% (rangoli design line) | Happy Diwali | Thu 28 Oct |
| Friends' group | tu / yaar | 6 of 20 words, 30% (kaju katli toss line) | Happy Diwali | Fri 29 Oct, evening |
| Partner | tum | 8 of 20 words, 40% (same balcony line) | Either | Fri 29 Oct, after diyas |
| Office group | aap | 6 of 19 words, 32% (late-night deadlines line) | Happy Diwali | Thu 28 Oct, office hours |

English runs from 12% for parents to 40% for a partner. Parents get the most Hindi because respect sits in the Hindi verb endings; the office line borrows English for work words and keeps *aap* for politeness.

## Turning a Hinglish wish into a Diwali card on SubhSandesh

A text wish suits a group chat; for one person who matters, the same Hinglish line can become the letter inside a card. [SubhSandesh's interactive Diwali card](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-diwali) takes a wish for each diya in a row, a tag on the diya at their door and a letter sealed in a red-and-gold shagun liffafa, in whatever mix of Hindi and English you text in. It has love, family and friend modes, up to six photos in sky lanterns, and opens from a private link in any phone browser with no app.

Since 48.3% of SubhSandesh pages are opened on a phone, keep each diya wish to one short line. If the person is a partner in another city, our [I miss you page for a long-distance partner](https://subhsandesh.in/missyou-gf) may fit better than a Diwali card. It is not a Diwali template, and its data is only two months old (n = 214 pages since 28 July 2026), but 43.5% of its senders add a password before sharing, against 38.5% of creators across the whole platform (measured 24 and 25 September 2026).

## When a Hinglish Diwali wish is the wrong choice

Hinglish is the wrong register for a grandparent who reads Hindi only in Devanagari; write शुभ दीपावली (Shubh Deepawali) in Devanagari instead. It is also wrong for a colleague who does not speak Hindi, where a mixed line excludes rather than warms, so send plain English.

SubhSandesh is the wrong tool in its own way. A card is one-to-one, so it cannot replace one message to a 40-person family group, and with 49.4% of Raksha Bandhan 2026 pages built on the day itself (our nearest analogue, n = 89), leaving a card until Lakshmi Puja evening is cutting it fine. Send the group the text line; build the one card on Dhanteras.

## Sources

- Sahni, A., *Bhasha* 4(1), 1 July 2025: Hinglish and the Matrix Language Frame model.
- Roark, B. et al., LREC 2020: the Dakshina romanisation dataset.
- Bali, K. et al., Workshop on Computational Approaches to Code Switching, 25 October 2014: Hindi-English mixing on Facebook.
- Wiktionary Hindi entries for शुभकामना and मुबारक, read 22 October 2026.
